extracted.intended_audience: students learning news writing / journalism reporters-in-training
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter of a news-writing textbook containing practice exercises and editorial directives for paragraphing, grammar, sentence structure, and coherence aimed at improving news copy. Learners are asked to identify and correct specific faults (pronouns, verbs, coordination, ellipsis) and to restructure sentences and paragraphs for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphing (where to break paragraphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate the places at which paragraphs should be made in the following stories:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises provide full news-story examples (e.g., CHARACTER INDICATED BY THE LIPS; FASHION MODEL MARRIES ALL IN BLACK) and ask the student to mark appropriate paragraph breaks. Implicit guidance: paragraph breaks should reflect changes in topic, time, scene, speaker, or emphasis; separate distinct ideas or developments in a story. (Several full stories are provided as practice material.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun usage — identify and correct faults
rubrics_metrics.description: The following sentences contain pronouns incorrectly used. Indicate and correct the faults in each sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus areas illustrated by numbered examples include pronoun-antecedent agreement, case (subject/object), number (singular/plural), gender reference, and ambiguous or inappropriate pronoun reference. Numerous example sentences (A.1–A.24) demonstrate common newsroom errors for correction and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb usage — correct verbs (agreement and tense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct the verbs in the following sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises target subject–verb agreement, correct tense and aspect usage, misplaced participles, and logical verb forms (e.g., plural vs. singular, auxiliary usage). Examples (B.1–B.18) show typical mistakes reporters make when writing leads and body copy that must be fixed for grammatical accuracy and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination and subordination — fix sentence structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The following sentences illustrate faults in coordination and subordination. Correct the errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students must reorganize or rewrite sentences so that clauses are properly coordinated or subordinated (parallel structure, logical relationships, avoiding run-ons and comma splices). Numbered examples (C.1–C.21) illustrate problems like mismatched constructions, faulty lists within quotes, and sentences that fail to show correct hierarchical relationships between ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis — correct errors due to faulty ellipsis
rubrics_metrics.description: The following sentences contain errors due principally to faulty ellipsis. Point out the faults in ellipsis and correct all errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on omitted words or constructions that create ambiguity or grammatical error in news sentences (e.g., missing auxiliaries, dropped antecedents). Examples (D.1–D.14) provide practice identifying where omission harms meaning and restoring the necessary words or rephrasing to eliminate ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence reconstruction for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconstruct the following sentences in any way that will make them clear. Point out the errors in the sentences as they now stand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises (E.1–E.30) ask students to rewrite awkward, ambiguous, or ungrammatical sentences so they are clear and readable — addressing misplaced modifiers, tangled clause sequences, faulty references, and confusing chronology. Emphasis is on producing clear, concise news-style prose while preserving facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite sentences to improve coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite the following sentences in any way that will improve their coherence (mainly paragraphs 163-164):
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks (F.1–F.15) require reworking sentences and short paragraphs to improve logical flow, remove redundant or contradictory phrases, correct mixed metaphors, and make narrative or descriptive sequences coherent and idiomatic for news copy. Examples demonstrate smoothing of transitions, pruning of redundancy, and tightening of phrasing for reader comprehension.
